title: Downtown Parking Master Plan and reduced residential parking
subtitle: Also: strong mayor powers governance updates, refreshed territorial acknowledgment, and closed-session riverfront park acquisition discussion.
overview: The committee spent most of the meeting on the Downtown Parking Master Plan. It recommended that Council approve the plan, including the tax-supported funding model, which keeps on-street parking free for now. It also recommended that staff develop a payment-in-lieu of parking program, and that paid on-street parking be reconsidered in the 2028 plan update. The committee heard the plan as a statutory public meeting on a proposed cut to the residential parking minimum in the downtown zones. The zoning decision was referred to the September 26 Council meeting {{vote:m6}}.

The committee also recommended a refreshed territorial acknowledgment for the City {{vote:m4}}. On consent, it advanced governance updates linked to the extension of strong mayor powers. These include changes to the Procedure By-law and Code of Conduct, a report on a lobbyist registry in early 2024, and amended budget meeting dates.

Council went into closed session on the Downtown Riverfront Park acquisition plan. The mayor reported afterward that staff direction was given, with no further detail. Because this was a committee meeting, Council must still adopt these recommendations. Staff will bring back a memo before then, so the parking decisions could change.

decisions.detail: The committee recommended that Council approve the plan with the tax-supported funding model (Scenario #2), keeping the existing approach to funding downtown parking.
The committee recommended that staff develop a payment-in-lieu program and by-law, and amend the reserve policy to create a Parking Payment-in-lieu Reserve Fund (303).
The committee recommended that staff report back on paid on-street parking after each Downtown Infrastructure Renewal street reconstruction, as part of the 2028 plan update.
The committee received the statutory public meeting report and referred the decision on the downtown residential parking zoning amendments to the September 26 Council meeting.
The committee recommended that Council approve the refreshed Territorial Acknowledgement for the City of Guelph.
On consent, the committee recommended approving the amended Procedure By-law, Code of Conduct and CAO and officer recruitment policies, and directed a report on a lobbyist registry in Q1 2024.

debate: Delegates were split on residential parking. A development consultant said the cut from 1.0 to 0.85 spaces per unit does not go far enough. The consultant asked that the pre-1971 exemption for converting existing buildings to housing be extended to buildings built before April 2023, arguing that parking costs make conversions unviable. A cycling coalition delegate also wanted deeper cuts, and wanted incentives to shift drivers from street parking to the underused parkades.

Staff said 0.85 reflects surveyed actual use in downtown buildings. They said site-specific reductions remain possible for affordable housing or developments with transit passes and car share. Staff warned that residents without parking could take spaces from visitors and employees. Staff also noted that the new Zoning By-law is under appeal at the Ontario Land Tribunal, and said the province has directed the city to reduce downtown parking.

Several councillors wanted to go further. One said parking minimums add to housing costs and urged removing them. Another asked for no parking requirements for affordable and supportive housing now, rather than waiting for the payment-in-lieu program. Others urged caution, citing spillover parking, Conestoga College's arrival and downtown construction. One opposed a blanket exemption because it removes the city's leverage to negotiate affordability.

On funding, one councillor said keeping on-street parking free is hard to square with climate goals, and that the wording about only investigating paid parking in 2028 shows the city drifting from the idea. Staff said it is the wrong time because of downtown disruption and fragile businesses. A caller said parking should pay for itself.

On the territorial acknowledgment, one councillor asked whether the phrase about being guests includes people whose families have lived in Guelph for generations. Staff said it reflects respect for the land and that a more personal version is planned for informal settings. Staff said the Métis Nation did not take part after outreach, and had earlier said they hold no land claims here.
